record.paper_title: The Interiors of Uranus and Neptune: Current Understanding and Open Questions
record.original_question: Which parts of Uranus and Neptune are superadiabatic, meaning regions where a steeper-than-adiabatic temperature gradient is needed to drive convective motion, and how do condensable species such as methane, hydrogen sulfide, and water in the middle and deep atmospheres change the temperatures inferred for the deeper interiors?

evidence.quote: Key fundamental questions regarding Uranus and Neptune remain open, such as: Key questions regarding Uranus and Neptune include: +What parts of each planet are superadiabatic?

Condensation into clouds removes these molecules from the gas phase, which alters the mean molecular weight of the atmosphere across the relatively narrow thickness of the cloud. This may lead to a number of regions of the middle and deep atmosphere becoming superadiabatic, as a steeper temperature gradient would be needed to drive convective motion.
The connection with the planetary interior is that these atmospheric superadiabatic regions would lead the deep interior to be hotter than previous simple estimates.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a giant ice-planet model of Uranus and of Neptune, idealized as a spherically symmetric fluid body in hydrostatic equilibrium with pressure P(r), temperature T(r), density ρ(r), and a mixture of hydrogen, helium, and condensable volatiles (notably methane CH4, hydrogen sulfide H2S, and water H2O). Define the adiabatic temperature gradient ∇_ad = (∂ ln T/∂ ln P)_S and the actual gradient ∇ = d ln T/d ln P. A region is called superadiabatic if ∇ > ∇_ad; in such a region a steeper-than-adiabatic temperature gradient is required to maintain convective heat transport, typically because condensation of a heavy species across a cloud layer increases the mean molecular weight μ with depth and stabilizes the layer against ordinary convection (the Ledoux criterion ∇ > ∇_ad + (φ/δ) ∇_μ, where ∇_μ = d ln μ/d ln P, must be satisfied for convection).

(a) Determine, as a function of radius (or pressure), which layers of Uranus and which layers of Neptune are superadiabatic. In particular, identify all condensation levels of CH4, H2S, and H2O in the middle and deep atmospheres at which a positive jump in mean molecular weight forces ∇ > ∇_ad, and characterize the resulting stably stratified or double-diffusive (semiconvective) layers.

(b) Quantify how the presence of these superadiabatic condensation layers modifies the temperature profile T(r) inferred for the deep interior, relative to the standard fully-adiabatic interior model anchored at the 1-bar level. Specifically, give the increase ΔT_deep in deep-interior temperature as a function of the assumed deep abundances of CH4, H2S, and H2O and of the thicknesses of the corresponding superadiabatic layers, and discuss the consequences for the equation of state, the inferred bulk composition, and the thermal evolution (luminosity) of each planet.
artifact.status_search_result: The identification of superadiabatic regions in Uranus and Neptune and the quantitative effect of condensable species (CH4, H2S, H2O) on inferred deep-interior temperatures remains an active open problem in ice-giant interior modeling. Recent work (e.g., Markham & Stevenson, Friedson & Gonzales, Scheibe et al., Vazan & Helled) has explored stably stratified moist layers and superadiabatic gradients but has not produced a definitive layer-by-layer determination, and the topic is highlighted as open in upcoming Uranus-mission science motivations.

status_evidence.title: Markham & Stevenson — Stable layers in giant planets
status_evidence.snippet: Condensation of heavy volatiles can produce stably stratified, superadiabatic layers in ice giants, but the locations and thicknesses remain uncertain.
status_evidence.claim: Existence and extent of superadiabatic layers in Uranus/Neptune is still being modeled, not resolved.

status_evidence.title: Scheibe, Nettelmann & Redmer — Thermal evolution of Uranus and Neptune
status_evidence.snippet: Allowing for non-adiabatic interiors substantially changes inferred deep temperatures and luminosity histories of the ice giants.
status_evidence.claim: Deep-interior temperatures depend strongly on assumed superadiabatic regions; quantitative answer is not settled.
